fullPassage: By limiting our marketing messages to external problems, we neglect a principle that is costing us thousands and potentially millions of dollars. That principle is this: companies tend to sell solutions to external problems, but people buy solutions to internal problems. The purpose of an external problem in a story is to manifest an internal problem. If I wrote a movie about a guy who simply needed to disarm a bomb, audiences would lose interest. What storytellers and screenwriters do, then, is create a backstory of frustration in the hero's life. In the movie Moneyball, for instance, Billy Beane failed in his playing career and so was filled with self-doubt about whether he could prove himself as a general manager. In Star Wars, Luke Skywalker was told by his uncle that he was too young to join the Rebellion, so he doubted his ability until the very end. In almost every story the hero struggles with the same question: Do I have what it takes? This question can make them feel frustrated, incompetent, and confused. The sense of self-doubt is what makes a movie about baseball relatable to a soccer mom and a romantic comedy relatable to a male truck driver. Stories teach us that people's internal desire to resolve a frustration is a greater motivator than their desire to solve an external problem. This is where most brands make a critical mistake. By assuming our customers only want to resolve external problems, we fail to engage the deeper frustration they're feeling. The truth is, it's those frustrations that are motivating them to call you.

questions.passage: By limiting our marketing messages to external problems, we neglect a principle that is costing us thousands and potentially millions of dollars. That principle is this: companies tend to sell solutions to external problems, but people buy solutions to internal problems. The purpose of an external problem in a story is to manifest an internal problem. If I wrote a movie about a guy who simply needed to disarm a bomb, audiences would lose interest. What storytellers and screenwriters do, then, is create a backstory of frustration in the hero's life. In the movie Moneyball, for instance, Billy Beane failed in his playing career and so was filled with self-doubt about whether he could prove himself as a general manager. In Star Wars, Luke Skywalker was told by his uncle that he was too young to join the Rebellion, so he doubted his ability until the very end. In almost every story the hero struggles with the same question: Do I have what it takes? This question can make them feel frustrated, incompetent, and confused. The sense of self-doubt is what makes a movie about baseball relatable to a soccer mom and a romantic comedy relatable to a male truck driver. Stories teach us that people's internal desire to resolve a frustration is __________ than their desire to solve an external problem. This is where most brands make a critical mistake. By assuming our customers only want to resolve external problems, we fail to engage the deeper frustration they're feeling. The truth is, it's those frustrations that are motivating them to call you.

questions.stem:
주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?

By limiting our marketing messages to external problems, we neglect a principle that is costing us thousands and potentially millions of dollars.

(A) That principle is this: companies tend to sell solutions to external problems, but people buy solutions to internal problems. The purpose of an external problem in a story is to manifest an internal problem.

(B) If I wrote a movie about a guy who simply needed to disarm a bomb, audiences would lose interest. What storytellers and screenwriters do, then, is create a backstory of frustration in the hero's life.

(C) In the movie Moneyball, for instance, Billy Beane failed in his playing career and so was filled with self-doubt about whether he could prove himself as a general manager. In Star Wars, Luke Skywalker was told by his uncle that he was too young to join the Rebellion, so he doubted his ability until the very end.

det.korean: 마케팅 메시지를 외적 문제로만 한정함으로써, 우리는 수천, 심지어 수백만 달러의 손실을 초래하는 원칙을 간과한다. (A) 그 원칙은 이것이다: 기업은 외적 문제에 대한 해결책을 팔려 하지만, 사람들은 내적 문제에 대한 해결책을 산다. (B) 만약 내가 그저 폭탄을 해체해야 하는 남자에 관한 영화를 썼다면, 관객들은 흥미를 잃을 것이다. (C) 영화 Moneyball에서, Billy Beane은...
det.analysis:
①(A)-(B)-(C)✅(주어진 글에서 언급된 'a principle'을 (A)가 구체적으로 설명하고, (B)가 스토리텔러들이 왜 내적 문제를 만드는지 설명한 뒤, (C)가 Moneyball과 Star Wars의 구체적 예시로 마무리하는 자연스러운 흐름)
②(B)-(A)-(C)❌((B)가 먼저 나오면 앞의 'a principle'을 받을 대상이 없어 흐름이 끊김)
③(C)-(A)-(B)❌(구체적 예시인 (C)가 원칙 설명 (A)보다 먼저 나올 수 없음)
④(B)-(C)-(A)❌((A)의 원칙 설명이 맨 뒤로 가면 전체 논리가 역전됨)
det.tip: 지시어 'That principle'이 가리키는 내용이 바로 앞 문장에 있는지 확인하여 (A)의 위치를 먼저 고정한다.

This is where most brands ②<u>make</u> a critical mistake. By assuming our customers only want to resolve external problems, we fail ③<u>to engage</u> the deeper frustration they're feeling. The truth is, it's those frustrations ④<u>what</u> are motivating them to call you.
